articles.title: Bangladesh needs COP31 to deliver clarity on climate finance
articles.description: Bangladesh cannot bear rising climate costs alone - the UN climate summit in Antalya must show how timely, accessible finance will be delivered at the scale needed
paragraphs: Shaikh Faridul Islam MP is Bangladesh 's State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

Bangladesh arrived at COP31 having committed substantial public resources to protecting our people from climate change. Yet the costs continue to rise, leaving us to finance recovery from one disaster while preparing for the next.

We came to Antalya to communicate our communities' needs. Yet, so far, conversations in Antalya with developed countries on finance have not reflected the needs of developing countries. As we enter the final days of negotiations at COP31, this must change.

Any success at COP31 will depend on how key finance issues, including the tripling of adaptation finance, and our asks that frontline communities can access finance promptly and on terms that do not deepen their debt, are addressed. COP31 has made good progress on several issues, but progress for developing countries will be meaningful only if it is accompanied by progress on finance.

For developing countries like Bangladesh, this is essential. A coastal district needs a grant to secure drinking water before the dry season. A family that has lost its home needs support while it can still rebuild in its community. A factory installing rooftop solar needs a loan it can afford to repay. Each faces a different barrier, and countries can address all three by engaging constructively through formal negotiations on the Climate Finance Work Programme.

articles.title: Former Climate Diplomats Blame Three Nations for Research Funding Stalemate
articles.description: At the United Nations COP31 climate change conference, experts warn that political attacks could undermine the basis for future agreements.
paragraphs: ANTALYA, Turkey—The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change , established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.

But three countries—Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption—are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.

Those countries “are doing everything they can to slow the process,” Tubiana said. They are becoming less discreet about their efforts, she said, as they increasingly view their economies as threatened by a conditional agreement to transition away from coal, oil and gas reached during COP28, the 2023 Conference of the Parties conference in Dubai.

The science panel’s current impasse is especially troubling, “because we know climate problems are accelerating, and we need a lot of data and communication to understand what’s happening at this COP,” said Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and former United Nations special envoy on climate change.

Robinson said this isn’t the first time countries have tried to obstruct science. Recent examples include attacks seeking to undermine a recent United Nations Environment Programme report on “overshoot,” which concludes that there is no way to avoid passing the 2.7 degree Fahrenheit warming target in the Paris Agreement.

articles.title: NASA Researchers Create 3D Maps of California to Assess Wildfire Risk
articles.description: NASA researchers have produced detailed 3D topography maps for all of California, down to the scale of a single tree.
paragraphs: Lidar-derived 3D point cloud data acquired in 2020 over a wildland-urban interface in Santa Clara County, California. NASA/Daniel Dixon
NASA researchers have produced detailed 3D topography maps for all of California, down to the scale of a single tree.

NASA’s Wildfire, Ecosystem Resilience, and Risk Assessment Initiative team used airborne lidar, a technology that uses a pulsed laser to measure distances, with data collected by the U.S. Geological Survey’s 3D Elevation Program to create a consistent statewide map, with a pixel size of one square meter (about 1.2 square yards). By comparison, most space-based lidar data have a resolution of 10 to 25 square meters per pixel.
Scientists use lidar, which stands for light detection and ranging, to create comprehensive 3D maps of forests, cities, and even distant planets and moons.

The NASA Wildfire, Ecosystem Resilience, and Risk Assessment Initiative team, in collaboration with partners at the California Natural Resources Agency and California Air Resources Board, hopes to use these high-resolution maps to develop products that help assess wildfire risk, protect wildlife and ecosystems, and manage natural resources across California.

articles.title: World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31
articles.description: Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process
paragraphs: The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit .

“We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Expressing the frustration shared by scores of developing countries and thousands of civil society activists at these talks, he added: “They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”

Countries have only two official days of negotiation left at Cop31 to resolve key issues, such as whether the conference should recognise the need to “transition away from fossil fuels” and how to address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond the 1.5C of heating targeted in the Paris agreement .

The Australian presidency of the talks and the Turkish hosts convened a “divan” meeting of ministers on Wednesday evening . Named for the Ottoman empire’s term for a council or assembly, the aim of the meeting was to make progress on a revised draft of a possible outcome and find compromises on sticking points. Significant dividing lines remain on issues such as climate finance, how to ensure a “just transition” to clean economy jobs for workers in fossil fuels and helping poor countries adapt to the impacts of extreme weather.

The first draft of a “cover decision” , issued on Monday, contained 144 separate items, including several – such as the “transition away from fossil fuels” – that some of the nearly 200 countries at the fortnight-long talks find contentious. There are concerns that the Australian approach of including “everything” in the draft text may result in longer negotiations. A new draft is expected on Thursday morning.

A breakthrough from the “divan” meeting was not expected, but negotiators told the Guardian that countries were working together on compromises. Campaigners feared that the outcome would be feeble, however.

“Rich countries are offering crumbs to the adaptation fund, while blocking the negotiations that should provide the money countries need,” he said. “Listening to ministers praise the adaptation fund before giving next to nothing, you have to wonder how they expect it to do the work they say is so important.”

There was anger, too, over the “just transition mechanism” , which is intended to help developing countries ensure workers in high-carbon industries can be retrained or helped, while they grow nascent green industries. “We’re seeing massive steps backwards on adaptation finance and just transition, relative to previous Cops,” said Brandon Wu, the director of policy and campaigns at the ActionAid USA charity. “In both cases, the blocking is being led by the EU.”

articles.title: ¿Cuáles son los continuos efectos de El Niño para el Caribe y Latinoamérica?
articles.description: Estamos enfrentando un El Niño histórico y debemos prepararnos para clima extremo como sequías e inundaciones
paragraphs: Sudamérica y Centroamérica deben prepararse para riesgos distintos durante las próximas fases de desarrollo de El Niño . El término El Niño es parte de un fenómeno más amplio denominado El Niño–Oscilación del Sur, o ENSO. Se trata del principal modo de variabilidad climática interanual del planeta, es decir, uno de los mecanismos naturales más importantes por los cuales el océano y la atmósfera intercambian energía y reorganizan el clima global de un año a otro.

El déficit de lluvia y el calor pueden comprometer el agua, la agricultura y la energía en unos territorios, mientras que las lluvias abundantes elevan el peligro de inundaciones en otros. La intensidad del fenómeno en el Pacífico ecuatorial modifica esas probabilidades, pero no determina por sí sola la magnitud de los daños locales.

En Ecuador y el noroeste del Perú, el calentamiento del Pacífico oriental puede favorecer lluvias intensas durante la temporada húmeda, con peligro de inundaciones y deslizamientos. Para el sur de Brasil y sectores de la cuenca del Río de la Plata, incluidos territorios de Argentina, Uruguay y Paraguay, deben vigilarse los posibles excesos de lluvia y las crecidas. La nota técnica de la Organización de Estados de América destaca riesgos contrastantes de sequía, inundaciones y deslizamientos y pide anticipar sus consecuencias hídricas, energéticas y alimentarias. El total de lluvia, su concentración y el estado previo de las cuencas deben orientar la respuesta. Un pronóstico trimestral no permite identificar la fecha, localización o severidad de una tormenta particular.

El pronóstico del Centro de Predicción Climática de NOAA del 8 de octubre de 2026 señala que El Niño continúa fortaleciéndose y asigna una probabilidad superior al 83 % de que mantenga una intensidad fuerte a muy fuerte durante enero–marzo de 2027. Otro de los indicadores es el Índice Oceánico Relativo de El Niño ( RONI por sus siglas en inglés), que estima que la temperatura podría superar +2.5 °C en octubre–diciembre de 2026 para el Pacífico.

El boletín de NOAA respalda la posibilidad de una magnitud excepcional dentro del registro desde 1950, pero no demuestra que ya se haya alcanzado un récord. Tampoco permite fijar diciembre o enero como fecha segura del máximo. El pico oceánico, la duración del episodio y la culminación de sus efectos hidrológicos son momentos diferentes.

El Niño es la fase cálida de un sistema acoplado entre el océano y la atmósfera. El debilitamiento de los alisios y el desplazamiento de las lluvias tropicales hacia el Pacífico central y oriental modifican la circulación atmosférica y transmiten su influencia a regiones distantes. No es suficiente observar agua cálida: debe existir una respuesta atmosférica coherente. Cada episodio presenta diferencias, de modo que una señal oceánica más intensa no implica daños proporcionalmente mayores en todos los países.

La distribución del calentamiento entre las distintas regiones influye en la configuración de los efectos de El Niño, junto con la respuesta atmosférica y la época del año. En las regiones uno y dos, que habitualmente se analizan conjuntamente, el calentamiento frente a Ecuador y el norte del Perú puede favorecer lluvias intensas, inundaciones y deslizamientos en sus zonas costeras. Cuando el calentamiento abarca las otras regiones pueden modificarse las lluvias en amplios sectores de Centroamérica y Sudamérica: aumentar en el sur de Brasil y sectores de Argentina, Uruguay y Paraguay, especialmente en la cuenca del Río La Plata, y disminuir en Colombia, Venezuela, sectores del norte de Brasil y la Amazonía, así como en el Corredor Seco centroamericano y sectores del Pacífico de Costa Rica. En Chile central, la señal de mayores precipitaciones se asocia principalmente con el invierno austral. El calentamiento en la región Niño 4, situada más al oeste, también puede modificar la circulación atmosférica y la distribución de los impactos a distancia.

articles.title: Ocean advocates warn COP31 agreement should not be read as geoengineering boost
articles.description: The COP31 cover decision draft text include a controversial goal to increase carbon dioxide removal, which ocean advocates say could impact ecosystems
paragraphs: With COP31 set to agree that governments should do more to protect the oceans, climate campaigners and diplomats have warned that this must not be interpreted as encouragement for "unproven" marine-based geoengineering techniques.

Oceans absorb about 30% of the world's planet-warming carbon dioxide, reducing the impacts of climate change. Initial research suggests that they could absorb more if altered with through techniques like ocean alkalinity enhancement or ocean iron fertilisation, where iron is put in the ocean so that algae grows on it and sucks up carbon.

The initial draft of the COP31 cover text contains a goal to increase carbon dioxide removal in general. Some ocean advocates said the link between this and oceans has not and should not be made. This language is contentious, with the EU opposed, and may not be in the final decision.

Initial research suggests that they could absorb more if altered with through techniques like ocean alkalinity enhancement or ocean iron fertilisation, where iron is put in the ocean so that algae grows on it and sucks up carbon.

The initial draft of the COP31 cover text contains a goal to increase carbon dioxide removal in general. Some ocean advocates said the link between this and oceans has not and should not be made. This language is contentious, with the EU opposed, and may not be in the final decision.

A political call to action released yesterday by COP31 co-presidency Türkiye encourages countries to protect marine ecosystems like mangroves and seagrasses, recognising their carbon storage potential, but it avoids any mention of marine geoengineering techniques.

At a COP31 press conference on Tuesday, Palau’s ambassador Ilana Seid said her Pacific country supported strong language on the protection of oceans but is concerned about marine carbon dioxide removal. “A lot of the science there is unproven and we are cautioning against that,” she said.

The main deal being negotiated in Antalya is the first one since the release of a major scientific report by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) saying that overshooting the 1.5C temperature limit is now unavoidable and that, to bring temperatures back down, some technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere will be needed.

Seid added that, while some CDR will be necessary, it should be "at the tail end of the equation" and should not become a substitute for reducing emissions, an argument echoed by UNEP's chief Inger Andersen at an event in Antalya.

articles.title: Business Council of Australia more aligned with fossil fuel industry than its members’ values, analysis finds
articles.description: Research by InfluenceMap raises questions about association’s policies and representation, particularly around advocacy for new gas supplies
paragraphs: The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies.

The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over how its policies are shaped and whose interests they represent.

Analysis by the London-headquartered InfluenceMap found the BCA’s positions aligned more closely with energy companies Woodside, Santos and ConocoPhillips than with the majority of its corporate base, particularly on the energy transition, where it has advocated for new gas supplies over phasing down.
InfluenceMap’s Australia lead, Jack Herring, said major associations such as the BCA are an influential voice in government policymaking.
“These findings suggest the BCA’s climate policy engagement better reflects the narrow interests of members connected to the fossil fuel value chain than its wider membership,” Herring said.

“Advocacy for fossil gas expansion risks undermining Australia’s climate targets and also threatens to create increased health risks and energy affordability and security concerns for everyday households, so this is an issue that affects us all.”

InfluenceMap’s analysis of company positions shows more than two-thirds of the members assessed, including Qantas, Woolworths, Coles, Atlassian, Fortescue and major banks CBA and NAB, advocate for stronger climate policies than the business council itself.
That support typically includes backing faster renewable energy rollout and advocating for more ambitious emission reduction targets.

For the study, the thinktank assessed 58 companies – a representative sample of the BCA’s more than 120 members – drawing on thousands of public statements, government submissions and regulatory filings.

articles.title: Republicans could expedite bill to make big oil immune to lawsuits, warn experts
articles.description: GOP lawmakers are rushing through high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in
paragraphs: Climate groups fear lawmakers could pass a bill by the end of the year that would give fossil fuel companies immunity from lawsuits and legislation that aim to hold them accountable for the climate crisis.

After the blue wave election, Republican lawmakers are rushing to pass high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in. Hundreds of elected leaders and climate groups sent a letter to congressional Democratic leadership urging them to reject any proposal that would shield fossil fuel companies from liability for the climate crisis.

Iyla Shornstein, political director for the Center for Climate Integrity, said the election results showed voters don’t want this type of legislation. “Voters at the polls sent a clear message about how costs are impacting their everyday lives. Gas prices are skyrocketing, but why would we spend our time giving special treatment to big oil, who are also simultaneously enjoying record profits at our expense? … The elections sent a pretty clear message that our elected leaders need to be spending their time helping working families, not major corporations like big oil.”

In April, Republicans introduced the Stop Climate Shakedowns bill that would shield fossil fuel companies from various attempts to hold them accountable. Ted Cruz and Harriet Hageman, two Republican lawmakers, introduced companion Senate and House bills. “Radical environmental groups have waged a coordinated campaign to weaponize our judicial system against American energy producers, including many in Texas,” Cruz said in a statement announcing the Senate bill. “They’re using meritless lawsuits to bankrupt our energy industry, kill good-paying jobs and drive up the cost of electricity and gasoline for hardworking families.”

Eleven states, two tribal governments and dozens of municipalities have filed lawsuits against big oil companies to hold them accountable for the climate emergency. The lawsuits are grounded in science that connects climate disasters to emissions from fossil fuel companies and increasing evidence that the companies deceived the public about their own internal science warning them about the dangers of fossil fuels.

Another accountability effort has come from states such as New York and Vermont that have passed climate superfund laws to recover costs by shifting the financial burden from climate disasters on to the fossil fuel companies that caused them. Both New York and Vermont’s superfund laws have faced opposition including challenges by the Department of Justice; a judge struck down the New York superfund law in September, the state’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is appealing.

The fossil fuel immunity bill has four key parts, said Shornstein: it would dismiss existing climate liability lawsuits against fossil fuel companies, prohibit new lawsuits, void climate superfund laws and assert that the federal government is the sole authority over the regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and the climate crisis, which pre-empts states from acting on it.

articles.title: There’s a small chance climate change could reduce Atlantic hurricane activity. Here’s how.
articles.description: There are at least nine ways that global warming could reduce risks. But rising seas and continued coastal development could still make damage worse.
paragraphs: In 1914, the Atlantic experienced a stunning hurricane season: Only a single named storm formed, and it remained below hurricane strength.

Decades later, hurricane scientist Chris Landsea worked on a project to correct the 175-year-long Atlantic hurricane database. He was sure that when the team reviewed 1914, they would find evidence that other storms had occurred that year.
“But a thorough search of ship logs showed nothing, nada,” Landsea later reported at a hurricane conference, shrugging.
No other season before or since 1914 has approached that level of inactivity. But could something similar happen in the future?

On one hand, there’s plenty of reason to think that global warming will make hurricanes more frequent and severe: Hurricanes take heat energy out of the ocean and convert it to the kinetic energy of their winds. All things being equal, hotter oceans should enable more disturbances to grow into hurricanes — and for hurricanes to grow more powerful.

But hurricanes are fussy creatures, requiring a narrow set of conditions to prosper, including low wind shear (a term that refers to a change in wind speed or direction over a short distance), a moist atmosphere, a seed disturbance to get things started, and an unstable atmosphere — in other words, warm air near the surface and cold air aloft.

Perhaps surprisingly, most — but not all — computer models of future hurricane activity predict that the total number of named storms worldwide will decline because of global warming. An increase in atmospheric stability and dryness at mid-levels of the atmosphere could be a major factor, given that the tropical upper atmosphere is warming about one-and-a-half times as fast as the lower atmosphere.
A few other variables could plausibly lessen the hurricane threat in the future. I’ll get into the details below:

Keep in mind that even if all nine of these hurricane-suppressive factors occur, there are at least four unavoidable ways that hurricane scientists are confident that climate change will make hurricanes worse:

Weighing all these factors together, my hunch is that there is only about a 10% chance that climate change will cause a net reduction in Atlantic hurricane destruction over the coming 30 years compared to the past 30 years. And even if we get lucky, continued development along vulnerable coastal areas will increase the risk of hurricane damage.

articles.title: Want to reduce climate pollution from a rice field? Let it dry out periodically.
articles.description: Mitti Labs is using this method to help farmers in India reduce the environmental impacts of the staple grain.
paragraphs: Rice is typically grown in flooded fields because the rice plants can tolerate waterlogged conditions, but most weeds cannot.
Dalal: “It suffocates the weeds, which allows the rice shoots to take most of the nutrients and grow.”
But Devdut Dalal, cofounder of the company Mitti Labs , says keeping fields flooded uses a lot of water. That’s a concern in areas like India where water is increasingly scarce.
So his company is helping farmers in India adopt an alternate technique, in which they allow fields to dry out periodically over the growing season.
Mitti Labs uses AI, satellites, and on-the-ground data to monitor rice paddies and measure how much methane pollution farmers avoid by adopting this approach.
And they pay farmers for making the switch, with money raised by selling carbon credits to companies around the world looking to offset some of their own climate pollution.
So he says the model helps support rice farmers financially while reducing the environmental impact of producing this staple grain.

After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’?
articles.description: Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves
paragraphs: Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering.

Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home.
Today, 18 November, that intrepid traveler – Voyager 1 , a robotic space probe the size of a Mini Cooper – is exactly one light day away from us: 16.1bn miles.

No other human-made object has ever gone this far. Radio signals from Earth (traveling at the speed of light, 186,000 miles per second ) now take 24 hours to reach it, and another 24 hours to return. The return signals are so weak that scientists at Nasa’s Deep Space Network must use a massive satellite dish to hear them.

Nasa launched Voyager 1 in early September 1977, just weeks after the first Star Wars movie hit theaters with Luke Skywalker and his charming sidekick droid, R2D2. It took photos of the planets Jupiter and Saturn , then continued onward.

In 2012 it exited the sun’s protective shield of charged particles and magnetic fields, crossed a boundary called the heliopause , and entered interstellar space. That’s when it became a message in a bottle.

That message consists of a 12in, gold-plated copper disk engraved with information to showcase human culture and the diversity of life on Earth, should any advanced civilization discover it. The disk contains photos and greetings in 55 human languages, music by Mozart and Chuck Berry, the sound of a baby crying and a whale singing. It also has a time stamp and a map that orients the position of our solar system to 14 pulsars – dense remnants of massive stars – that rotate rapidly and emit beams of radiation like flashing cosmic lighthouses. The message says, in essence: this is where we live and who we are. We thrive on connection. Come see us sometime.

The astronomer Carl Sagan chaired a committee that designed the disk. In the late 1980s, as Voyager 1 hastened through the outer solar system, he tried to convince Nasa to turn the probe’s sensitive cameras back toward home.

Nasa resisted, concerned about the risk of instrument damage. Finally, on Valentine’s Day 1990, the cameras turned. The result was one of the most profound images ever captured in space exploration. Sagan called it the “ pale blue dot ”, wherein Earth appears as a fraction of a pixel, “like a mote of dust caught in a sunbeam”.

paragraphs: The imminent total destruction of the world’s coral reefs is not a scare story but a fact.
And it is predicted that within the next 25 years, coral reefs as we know them could be gone.

So ahead of COP31, it is Carry On Propaganda at the BBC, with ‘trusted’ Attenborough sending the kids to bed crying with an ancient climate scare that has no basis in observed reality. For 45 minutes, impressive high tech filming showing some of the wonders of the living ocean sets up the anxiety-inducing punch line. Needless to say, the terminal coral message is not sourced and is based on an unnamed “prediction” that “could” happen. Monbiot of course is beyond help, but even for Attenborough this is a new low – a pathetic attempt to pump up mass climate panic and psychosis across global populations.
But useful ahead of COP31 and welcomer news for the deluded attendees hoping to destroy current social and economic life on the blue planet with their collectivist Net Zero fantasy.

Ahead of the carefully planned Armageddon knockout punch, the Attenborough activist crew sets the scene in episode 1 of Blue Planet III by noting that the tropical seas are one of the richest habitats in the ocean. They have been bathed in sunlight for millions of years and more species live and thrive in these “hotspots” than anywhere else in the ocean. All this is true and tropical coral has thrived over vast areas in temperatures between 24°C to 32°C. But wait, cut the almost constant background whale music – the sort often heard in the nursery to comfort young babies – and cue the funereal score to announce “unprecedented” ocean heatwaves that are bleaching, starving and killing all the pretty coral. All could be gone within just 25 years, says Doleful Dave.

Coral destruction is a common scare that has been used for years by activists the world over. The fact that there have been numerous recent natural bleaching events at the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral structure in the world, yet coral has shown five years of record growth, is an inconvenient fact that destroys the ‘nice try, but no cigar’ termination twaddle. Quite how ocean ‘heatwaves’, a natural and common rise in surface temperature of 1-2°C lasting on average a mere 12 days , should suddenly kill all the coral that has survived everything nature has thrown at it for hundreds of millions of years is a complete mystery. Unless of course you are peddling some hard Left economic grab designed to impose ‘Big Brother’ control on human society.

Regular readers will be aware that Attenborough has previous form as long as your arm in peddling pseudoscientific climate agitprop that flies in the face of actual observations. In a 2022 Frozen Planet II broadcast, he claimed that the Arctic could be free of summer sea ice by 2035 . He was rather late to the game with this one, not least since the climate hysteric Al Gore never quite recovered his authority when he claimed the area could be ice free by 2014.

Back in the world of observational science, it is generally accepted that Arctic sea ice, summer and winter, has been stable for over 20 years . This popular climate scare was generally held to be on its last legs following a recent well publicised paper from Dr Mark England of the University of Exeter. Conceding the obvious, he noted a “surprising, but not unexpected pause”. Of course, it might be added that it was only surprising to those who get their information from computer models, and not unexpected for those who consult cyclical Arctic ice trends over decades rather than months.

articles.title: ‘Phantom forests’ in Australia’s arid outback used to create carbon credits meant to offset emissions, report claims
articles.description: Carbon credit companies reject research that found only small increase in forest and canopy cover in regeneration areas despite wet conditions
paragraphs: A fight over the legitimacy of Australia’s climate change policy has reignited after researchers claimed “phantom forests” in the semi-arid outback are being used to create offsets that allow fossil fuel companies to keep pumping out pollution.

A group of academics, including professors from the Australian National University and the University of New South Wales, said they had examined 50 forest regeneration projects used to create carbon credits.

Led by Prof Andrew Macintosh , the former federal government carbon credit scheme integrity chair and the director of ANU’s Centre for Environmental Markets, the researchers said they found only a small increase in forest and tree crown cover in the areas over the past five years despite wet conditions.

They said the conclusions were consistent with their previous peer-reviewed studies that found Australia’s method for creating carbon credits from forest regeneration was doing little to nothing to help address the climate crisis .

The research was published in a report released on Wednesday by the Australian Conservation Foundation. Prof David Eldridge, one of the report’s authors and a former principal research scientist with the NSW environment department, said he was “gobsmacked” that “phantom forests” in outback areas north-west of the remote town of Bourke could earn carbon credits for forest regrowth.

The findings were rejected by companies that manage what are known as human-induced regeneration projects in north-western NSW. “These are some of the most closely examined carbon projects in the country, and the evidence on the ground shows they are working,” a spokesperson for Green Collar, a business that manages carbon credit projects, said.
Each carbon credit is said to represent one tonne of emissions that has been removed from, or prevented from being released to, the atmosphere.

Their use is contentious, in part, because industrial-polluting companies that are required to cut emissions under a federal policy known as the safeguard mechanism are allowed to buy an unlimited number of credits to count as their own cuts while continuing to pollute.
Scientists have warned limiting the climate crisis requires rapid direct cuts in emissions and that carbon credits – also known as offsets – should be used sparingly .

articles.title: COP31 Bulletin Day 9: Crunch ministerial talks planned for Wednesday evening
articles.description: With a draft cover text still untrimmed, the presidency is holding a “Divan" meeting to make progress towards a "balanced package"
paragraphs: With just three official days of talks left, the catch-all initial draft of the cover decision - which the Arab Group and Russia say they reject - has yet to be slimmed down.
To speed things up, the COP31 presidency has asked governments to send their top people to a meeting at 5pm local time dubbed a “Divan”, a word derived from an Ottoman council.

There, they are being encouraged to respond to the question: “How can COP31 send signals and capture a clear plan of action which meets the moment, while respecting national circumstances and priorities?”

Participants are encouraged to speak directly to each other rather than just reading out statements to the chair, who - despite Australia’s role as President of Negotiations - will be COP31 President Murat Kurum.

The aim is to “explain where their delegations see room for common ground and what they would need to reach agreement” on a text that is intended to be the cherry on the cake of “a balanced package” including negotiated agenda items. A handful of observer groups will also be present in the room.
It is unclear whether the next version of the text will come out before or after the "Divan" meeting. The presidency has said only that it will be published as soon as possible.

Before then on Wednesday, we are expecting announcements from a group of countries aiming for net negative emissions and we will be hearing from the European Union again at a 2pm press conference. There will also be a ministerial event to launch the next Global Stocktake of national climate plans, which is due to conclude in 2028.

articles.title: In Western Pennsylvania, You Might Live Next to—or on Top of—an Unplugged Well
articles.description: Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette have built an interactive map to bring these old ghosts to light
paragraphs: Abandoned : The aging oil and gas wells haunting Pennsylvania. This project is a collaboration between Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.
There are six old oil wells within 150 feet of Brittany and Ryan Mahoney’s first house in the South Fayette neighborhood known as The Berkshires. They didn’t know about any of them.

The thousands of oil and gas wells that still linger underground in this region are often long forgotten up on the surface. Some wells were drilled more than a century ago, and many haven’t produced oil or gas in decades. Some have been plugged with tree trunks. Some are still cavities.

Many don’t pose any immediate health or safety risks, but there’s no easy way for residents to know if a nearby well is leaking gas, fouling groundwater, or otherwise reacting to all the other extraction activities going on underground. It’s especially hard to monitor any of those hazards if you don’t know where the wells are.

More than a hundred years ago, The Berkshires neighborhood was part of the most prolific oil play in the world, the McDonald Oil Field—so productive that its output was reported in gallons per minute.

articles.title: How and Why We Mapped Pennsylvania’s Forgotten Oil and Gas Wells
articles.description: They’re near and beneath homes, parks, businesses and more. Now you can learn more about them.
paragraphs: Abandoned : The aging oil and gas wells haunting Pennsylvania. This project is a collaboration between Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

Thanks to its long history of oil and gas exploration, the geology of Western Pennsylvania resembles a huge block of Swiss cheese. From the industry’s beginnings in 1859, when Edwin Drake struck oil less than 70 feet beneath the surface just south of Titusville, to the modern-day fracking boom that launched in 2004, hundreds of thousands of wells have been drilled into the landscape—adding to a labyrinth of shafts and tunnels from the region’s coal mines.

Many of these wells have long since been abandoned. Their operators may have gone out of business, if they are even known. Some old wells are still obvious from rusting wellheads and pipes. But in many cases, there’s little sign of them at the surface.

These wells are hidden in forests, shopping centers, even the Pittsburgh Botanic Garden. Others lie beneath the terminal and runways of the Pittsburgh International Airport. There could even be a hidden well in your backyard or beneath your home.

And while many of these wells pose little hazard beyond tripping over a protruding pipe, some may be leaking explosive methane, toxic carbon monoxide or carcinogens like benzene. Oil and gas wells can create air and water pollution. Exercise great care if you think a well may be nearby.
The state’s Department of Environmental Protection does provide an oil and gas well mapping tool . But it can be slow and difficult to use, especially if you’re not an expert.

articles.title: What the World’s First Oil Boom Left Behind
articles.description: America’s oil and gas industry was born in Pennsylvania. Hundreds of thousands of aging, unplugged wells are one of its enduring legacies.
paragraphs: Abandoned : The aging oil and gas wells haunting Pennsylvania. This project is a collaboration between Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

The property that became the Pittsburgh Botanic Garden has led many lives: coal mine, farmland, resurrected forest. Inside the southern boundary, in acres of dense woods off-limits to visitors, the relics of a less-remembered chapter litter the landscape.

Past the back gate is a jumble of overturned tanks, stained sheds and tangled, broken pipes. The creek gurgles strangely, a sulfurous smell hanging in the air. High on the ridge, rusted pumpjacks stand like quiet sentries. One wears a metal tag stamped with the name of a woman who lived here more than a century ago.

Jane McGill #1 is an abandoned oil well, drilled at the height of what was then the biggest oil rush in the world, and this is an oil field graveyard. The well is one of hundreds of thousands of oil and gas wells left unplugged by operators and scattered across the state, from Washington County in the southwest to Susquehanna in the northeast.

Some of them are fouling the air with methane, the highly flammable gas and potent climate pollutant, and other chemicals like cancer-causing benzene. In some cases, abandoned wells have been linked to home explosions. Others are implicated in water contamination, acting as accidental conduits between present-day drilling and private water wells.

For decades these lost wells went largely unnoticed. But dealing with them has become more urgent as suburbia sprawls into what used to be open space. Forgotten oil and gas wells now lurk near and even beneath shopping centers, schools, homes, backyards and public parks. They may no longer be marked, their metal casing stripped for scrap, the only sign a patch of dead grass, bubbles surfacing in a pond or an unassuming hole in the ground.

Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette set out to help make residents more aware of the wells in their midst. Using data from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, we built an interactive tool that allows users to input an address anywhere in the state and immediately see if active, abandoned or orphaned wells are nearby.

articles.title: Climate Diplomacy Brief
articles.description: Time and credit is running out for the Australian / Turkish COP hosts: as the pressure mounts will they stick or twist?
paragraphs: 72 hours Bright lights. Constant noise. Airless rooms. Average coffee. Tiredness is starting to seep into the bones and brains of envoys at COP31. Some have been existing on 5-6 hours sleep a night for the last 10 days. Managing teams. Analysing texts. Negotiating in Antalya and with capitals back home. The pressure is rising, inexorably. Türkiye and Australia did not have to have a major political decision, but they chose to. Officially less than 72 hours remain. Horror show That’s how Tuesday’s 4-6pm ‘heads of delegation’ meeting on Monday’s draft cover decision was described by one observer. That’s not unusual at this point in the second week when everything’s at stake. Below is a summary of views expressed by key blocks (not much has changed): *Arab Group: Remove ICJ, roadmaps, 1.5C work programme, electrification, IPCC timing *Islands: Backsliding on overshoot/1.5C is not on, too much CCUS + anti-science language *EU: Supports electrification target, focus on overshoot, dislikes historical responsibility *Africa: Supports 1.5C/overshoot language, more focus on adaptation + specifics on $$$ *Least Developed: Clarity on adaptation finance, supports ICJ reference *China: A text lacking coherent internal structure is like a body without bones - a zombie *Mex, Swiss, ROK: Supports 1.5C overshoot ref, wants more on fossil fuels transition AOSIS Chair Ambassador Ilana Seid took aim at “certain countries” who undermine the IPCC, calling out “scientists from a very select group of countries that have been sent here to brainwash us.”

Sitrep A generous take is the Australian/Bowen approach to this cover text was to allow for open discussion this week so everyone could present/vent their views. But, as ever with such a strategy, this carries risk: in this case an explosion of red lines and raw rage. Ministers will now engage on the details throughout Wednesday. articles.title: California Manure Lagoons Could Be ‘Ticking Time Bombs’ in the Forecasted Monster El Niño
articles.description: Regulators warned dairies to ready their animal waste ponds for storms that could bring the state at least 150 percent of its normal rainfall. Farmers say they’re preparing.
paragraphs: Countless manure lagoons on dairy farms across California’s San Joaquin Valley will be vulnerable to serious flooding during what is likely to be a fierce and historic El Niño this winter.

These pools of cow feces and urine are commonly how dairies store waste on-site. When the lagoons overflow, any number of contaminants in the solid and liquid slurry—which contains high concentrations of chloride and nitrogen as well as pathogens— can pollute the environment and communities nearby.
The San Joaquin Valley has upwards of 1,000 dairy farms, the most in any part of the state. The total number of waste lagoons in the valley and statewide—dairies can have more than one—is unknown.

The current El Niño , which will ramp up heading into December, could bring devastating flooding to waste lagoons, leading to environmental problems like contamination of drinking water and the spread of manure sludge through rural neighborhoods, experts warned.

It wouldn’t be the first time the weather phenomenon has battered the state. Along the coast and throughout Southern California, families and farmers saw record-breaking storms in the El Niños of 1982-83 and 1997-98. The current El Niño is likely the strongest in over a millennium, a recent study in Science found.

Three years ago, the San Joaquin Valley was pummeled by atmospheric rivers that forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of cows from dairy farms. How overflow from manure lagoons impacted the many rural communities that sit beside dairies is impossible to know, as a true accounting of the effects has never been completed.

articles.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31
articles.description: Editorial: Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability
paragraphs: “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis , ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation.

But is the world failing to tackle climate change because governments lack the political will? Or because climate action, among other development objectives, is being pursued within a global economic system whose rules entrench the inequalities inherited from colonialism? That is the question posed by Fadhel Kaboub , an economist at Denison University, Ohio, and adviser to the UN. His answer is that those structures never truly disappeared, but have evolved into today’s rules governing international finance, trade, investment and taxation. The upshot is that the countries least responsible for global warming have the fewest resources to confront its consequences.

At Cop31, Dr Kaboub was among a group of experts arguing for the least developed countries to emulate Mark Carney’s middle-power strategy and employ the same logic of collective bargaining in a world of great-power rivalry. Poorer nations should seek not just strategic autonomy but economic sovereignty. The experts suggested that they pool resources and build regional common markets as well as green industries together. The aim was to negotiate as a bloc with western powers – and China – for technology transfer and investment without racking up further debt. Half a century after developing nations demanded a new international economic order , the climate crisis may be giving that unfinished struggle a new purpose.

The New Rules of Permitting
articles.description: The permitting bill's most important clause doesn’t decide what gets built. It decides whose decisions last.
paragraphs: Last week, the Senate voted 73-25 to open debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or “BAAJA,” the biggest rewrite of federal permitting rules in a generation. It would speed approvals for everything from power lines to gas pipelines and make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need. Its sponsors are racing to pass the bill before Democrats take control of Congress in January, betting that this alignment of a bipartisan Senate deal, a Republican House and a president who backs the bill won’t come again. Last night, senators voted 70-27 to cut off debate on the revised bill , setting up a final vote as soon as this week.

BAAJA’s least-controversial section concerns power lines. Today, a single state can stall an interstate transmission line for years. Environmental reviews for transmission take more than twice as long as for gas pipelines , and the main federal process for planning lines between regions has produced zero miles of high-voltage line since it was created in 2011. BAAJA would let federal regulators approve a line if a state refuses or doesn’t act within a year, and require neighboring grid regions to plan lines together. Even the bill’s fiercest critics call this reform “excellent.”

But the more-controversial Section 1401 of the bill makes a finished permit very hard to take back. Agencies could revoke one only in narrow cases , such as fraud, a court order or an immediate threat to health or the environment. An agency that interferes in bad faith could owe the developer a quarter to half of what it has spent. That makes determining the bill’s climate impacts a question of timing and leadership.

The motivating case is obvious: In 2025, the Trump administration halted five offshore wind projects , one of them about 87 percent built. But the protection Section 1401 provides is fuel-blind. It covers pipelines, LNG terminals and mines just as fully as wind farms. And it affects any permit in effect on or after Nov. 6, so it starts protecting approvals already on the books, not just future ones.
Permit durability, in other words, is an amplifier. It strengthens whoever happens to be issuing permits.

That’s why the bill’s champions and critics can read the same clause and reach opposite conclusions. One of the bill’s authors, Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) argues that the bill cuts permitting for a major power line from about two decades to about five years—still too slow for President Donald Trump to finish much, so the next president collects. Earthjustice President Abigail Dillen argues the reverse : Favored industries of the current administration will rush to lock in approvals that no successor can undo.

Rich countries must step up to replenish Green Climate Fund, Duarte says

paragraphs: Wealthy nations are expected to take the lead in topping up the UN’s Green Climate Fund (GCF) over the coming year, even though using taxpayers’ money for international climate finance is a hard sell in today's political climate, the fund's head, Mafalda Duarte, told Climate Home News.

As the GCF kickstarts its replenishment push for the 2028-2031 period, many governments in rich countries are redirecting their overseas aid budgets towards domestic priorities, including military spending amid ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East .

At COP31 last week, the Solomon Islands made waves by becoming the first country to contribute to the GCF’s fourth fundraising round. It is also the first small island developing state (SID) and the first least developed country (LDC) to put money into the fund, which helps poorer nations cut their emissions and adapt to climate change.

In the last couple of years, wealthy governments have scaled back new commitments for international climate finance, and the UK has cut its current GCF contribution in half . articles.title: Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep
articles.description: I am at Cop31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices, says energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh
paragraphs: I n this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.

Yes, the world will overshoot 1.5C of global heating in the coming years. But without the Paris agreement, the world would have been on track for a 4C increase. International commitments, finance and adaptation are working, and multilateralism has never been more vital to our future. Every fraction of a degree we prevent means lives protected and communities given a better chance at surviving. Setbacks bring frustration, but resistance is the sign of progress.

Britain has a responsibility to lead, and we are determined to do so. I am proud of the progress we have made to cut emissions by 54% since 1990 and the action we are taking to achieve net zero by 2050 . And I am equally proud of our record on climate action abroad. We exceeded our five-year international climate finance commitment, spending £12.8bn between 2021-22 and 2025-26 against a pledge of £11.6bn. Britain exceeded its £3bn nature target and tripled annual adaptation funding from £500m to more than £1.5bn.

And the real measure of that investment is what it has achieved. Since 2011, UK climate finance has helped an estimated 159 million people across the world better adapt to the climate crisis, reduced or avoided 201m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions and mobilised about £26bn in public and private finance.

So, what next? At Cop31 , Britain will push for action. And what does that look like? A faster clean-energy transition, cuts to methane, protection for forests and oceans, and better access to finance. The drive for electrification, in particular, is a huge global opportunity. Investing in homegrown clean power is a win-win. It allows us to break our dependence on volatile fossil-fuel markets and protect families from price shocks, while reducing the carbon we use. And through the rollout of solar energy, batteries, clean heat and electric vehicles, communities in Britain will directly benefit from this energy transition through lower bills and a stake in the energy system of the future.

articles.title: Wildfire-prone areas could turn to microgrids to cope with power outages
articles.description: When wildfire risk is high, utilities sometimes shut off power lines, leaving people without electricity for days.
paragraphs: When it’s extremely windy and dry, and the risk of wildfire is high, utilities sometimes turn off certain power lines to prevent sparking a blaze.
Brooks: “I live in Boulder, Colorado. We had our power turned off for five days last December. … The only saving grace for us was that it was relatively temperate and so pipes weren’t freezing.”
That’s Cameron Brooks of the group Think Microgrid . He says microgrids can help prevent those outages.

A microgrid is an energy system that provides power to a building, a neighborhood, or an area like a college campus. It often includes solar panels and battery storage. And it’s connected to the larger electricity grid, but it can also disconnect and operate independently.
So microgrids can provide backup power when the grid goes down during storms or when utilities need to shut off power to specific lines.
Brooks: “Then the utility could safely deenergize those lines, avoid the risk of wildfire, without causing a disruption to service that people depend on.”
So microgrids can help build resilience in wildfire-prone areas while also expanding the use of clean, renewable energy.

Are Multibillion-Dollar Wildfire Payouts Undermining Efforts to Make Forests Less Flammable?
articles.description: Prescribed burners say the prospect of costly litigation and rising insurance rates are complicating efforts to fight fire with fire.
paragraphs: The small fire slowly licked its way through a dense growth of pine trees in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains of northern New Mexico. A team of federal employees moved in tandem with the flames, dropping more fire from drip torches to clear out the small trees, deadwood, scrub and grasses that could fuel a runaway blaze in the future. Everything seemed to be going to plan.

But come afternoon, strong winds swept into the burn area. Powerful gusts carried the carefully planned fire beyond the control line intended to contain it. By 5 p.m. on April 6, 2022, the U.S. Forest Service reported the burn had escaped its control and declared it a wildfire.

The Hermit’s Peak Fire would eventually merge with another prescribed burn that had survived the winter as a “sleeper” fire in nearby Calf Canyon. In January, the Forest Service had burned piles of tree trunks and limbs left over from previous forest-thinning operations. But embers from the pile burn had smoldered beneath the winter snow and the fire reemerged in the spring.

By the time the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire finally came under control in August 2022, the once-modest prescribed burns intended to reduce the potential for megafires in New Mexico had become the largest wildfire in the state’s history.

The colossal fire swept across more than 340,000 acres and destroyed more than 900 structures in San Miguel, Mora and Taos counties. Torrential rain in the fire’s burn scar spawned a flash flood that killed three people.
More than four years later, the fire’s memory has barely faded for those who witnessed the towering walls of flame. Outrage, too, has endured. How did a government-sanctioned project go so, so wrong?

articles.title: Twenty Years of Watts Up With That?
articles.description: Twenty years ago today, I started Watts Up With That with one simple blog entry. The idea was somewhat gee-whiz in nature. It did not stay that way for long.
paragraphs: Twenty years, over 600 million page views, over 38,000 articles, countless arguments, personal losses, and one stubborn idea: scientific claims should stand or fall on the evidence.

Twenty years ago, on November 17, 2006, I published the first post at Watts Up With That? . I had no grand plan to build one of the world’s most widely read climate-related websites. I certainly didn’t envision spending the next two decades examining temperature records, questioning climate models, debating scientists, dealing with the occasional internet mob, or explaining for the umpteenth time why a thermometer next to an air-conditioning exhaust might not be the ideal instrument for measuring long-term climate change. I thought I might finally have a little spare time. That prediction turned out to be spectacularly wrong, and considering the subject matter that would eventually dominate this website, there’s a certain irony in that.

The original idea behind WUWT was simple enough. I wanted a place to discuss interesting things about science, technology, weather, and the natural world. I described it as somewhat “gee-whiz” in nature. The internet already had plenty of celebrity gossip and political shouting matches, and I was more interested in the kind of useful trivia that makes people stop and think. Why is the sky blue during the day but black at night? Why does urine smell funny after eating asparagus? And, with apologies to Lon, does disc golf cause cancer? Those were the sorts of questions I thought we might explore. The only real ground rules were to avoid crude language and personal attacks. Otherwise, almost anything was fair game.

The blog began under the umbrella of the Chico Enterprise-Record’s NorCalBlogs platform, and my intended audience was largely local: people around Northern California who knew me from my days on television and shared my interest in science, weather, and technology. For the first few months, that’s pretty much what it was. I wrote about PlayStation 3s, internet speed tests , hurricane-strength nails, and household power hogs. Climate-related material appeared almost immediately, but WUWT was still primarily a general science and technology blog. That began to change in the spring of 2007, when a longstanding curiosity about weather instruments led me in an unexpected direction.

Before getting into that history, I should say a word about the feature image created for this anniversary by Charles Rotter. Charles has taken the familiar Stevenson screen, that traditional white wooden shelter used to house weather instruments, and given it a rather unusual architectural upgrade. It now resembles an outhouse, complete with a thermometer mounted on the door, standing alone in a field beneath a beautiful sunrise. The caption simply reads, “TWENTY YEARS — 2006–2026.”

I had to laugh when I first saw it. After two decades of examining the condition and placement of surface temperature stations, the image sums up rather neatly what we’ve thought about the quality of some of the measurements being used to construct the historical temperature record. The thermometer may be housed in something that looks vaguely official, but that doesn’t necessarily make the observations trustworthy. Of course, the cartoon is deliberately exaggerated, and the actual scientific questions are considerably more complicated. Still, Charles has managed to convey twenty years of frustration with poorly sited instruments in a single picture. Sometimes a little humor gets the point across more effectively than another hundred pages of statistical analysis. Thanks, Charles. It’s a fitting image for the occasion.

articles.title: A Landmark Deal Saved Colorado’s Roan Plateau. Now It’s Headed Back to the Auction Block.
articles.description: A new federal mandate requires fossil fuel lease auctions on land that past negotiations were supposed to have set aside, raising concerns about the fate of other public lands protections.
paragraphs: Almost a decade after a compromise between the Bureau of Land Management, conservationists and local governments safeguarded about 90 percent of the Roan Plateau in Western Colorado from gas drilling, those federal protections are being unraveled in the Trump administration’s push to open more public lands for resource extraction.

But in 2012, a U.S. District Court judge in Denver ruled the agency hadn’t followed proper protocol in developing the leasing plan and ordered that it be updated after the BLM conducted additional analysis of air quality impacts and considered an alternate plan, the “Community Alternative.” After two more years of litigation, the plaintiffs and the BLM reached a settlement in 2014 that canceled all but two leases on top of the plateau.
Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.
A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.
Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.
A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Those protections are now in doubt. The second Trump administration’s push to increase resource extraction on public lands has reopened the possibility of development on lands that were previously protected. This December, the Bureau of Land Management will offer four parcels atop the Roan as part of the quarterly statewide lease sales mandated by 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“There was such broad consensus on the ground in this local community to protect this very special place,” said Chris Winter, a natural resources and environmental lawyer who runs the University of Colorado Law School’s Getches-Wilkinson Center for Natural Resources, Energy, and the Environment. “And then the administration can come in and just override that local consensus. I think that should concern everybody across the West.”

“There’s nobody out here who lives out here who wants to ruin the land,” said Wade Haerle, Executive Director of Club 20, a Western Slope advocacy organization that promotes resource development as essential for area economies. “We have been in support of leasing it as soon as practical … and we firmly believe that hunting and fishing, and oil and gas, [are all appropriate uses of] public lands, and they can coexist together.”

The Roan Plateau rises 3,500 feet above the Colorado River Valley between De Beque and Rifle on Colorado’s Western Slope. It sits atop the southern margin of the Piceance Basin, one of the most heavily drilled natural gas fields in the West; the federal land at the center of the fight covers some 73,600 acres.

paragraphs: Ministers are in the building and embarking on the tricky task of refining the mammoth draft cover text down to something that can be agreed upon by the end of the week.

If the reactions heard so far at COP are anything to go by, this will be a big challenge. Few appear happy about its current form, with Europe’s climate commissioner dubbing it a “shopping list” on Tuesday and some large emerging economies rejecting the text outright.

According to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin, which unlike the media is allowed into the room, at a heads of delegation meeting on Monday evening, Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) - a group that includes China, India and Saudi Arabia - said the draft crosses their red lines.

Particularly, they object to the inclusion of the 35x35 electrification target, the roadmap on transitioning away from fossil fuels and calls to rapidly reduce methane. The Arab Group and Russia went further, rejecting the draft text entirely over similar concerns. Even Türkiye’s ally Azerbaijan criticised the draft, ENB reports.

The European Union also voiced doubts, saying it was not going in the right direction by including elements on finance, trade and carbon capture and storage. On the other hand, the text currently contains most of the EU’s key asks, including on responding to an overshoot of 1.5C and acknowledging the latest science.

Negotiations on the cover decision resume in this afternoon. Other developments of note include concerns about the fate of the Climate Finance Work Programme (CFWP), with the poorest countries wanting it to continue for two more years and include a goal to triple adaptation finance. The EU and Switzerland have called for no text on this item, not wanting to take on new financial commitments.

articles.title: They’re back: The mullahs of meteorology and climate
articles.description: In the end, to me, the weather and climate have to be stand-alones, and the other items are a response to them, not the reason for an answer.
paragraphs: I really wanted to be involved in the hierarchy that would help figure out how to address the climate agenda. I felt that, as someone who has been forecasting for over 50 years and relies on climate and past weather data, I could offer a different kind of input — one from the guy digging the ditch who has to deal with the fact that being wrong actually costs you something. I have always felt that the crucible of capitalism and competition will yield the best results. And certainly, in a private sector that has to compete for a shrinking dollar, you cannot simply dismiss anything that may impact the forecast.

But now I am glad I am not involved. And that is a horrible thing to say, because of the reason. It has to do with what I was warning my colleagues about at the climate conference back in April. You can’t win with zealots unless you take away the reason for the zealotry. And since it’s not really about climate and weather, but control, they were not going away. Now look at what we are seeing. The recent shift in Congress and the Senate has emboldened that extremity, so people are going to be targets. Some of those people may be held “accountable” for actions they took because they believed those actions were the best course of action. Of course, it’s not only people in the administration involved with climate and weather; it’s across the board.

I have always had a variety of clients. If a client happens to be an oil company that needs a forecast, I provide one. For instance, we have a colder December forecast than the standard strong El Niño analog. Even though December may not be cold compared to many others, it should be colder than that standard. Here is the example:
You start computing the difference in energy costs, and even though we’re by no means forecasting a frigid December — just one that’s not as warm — the difference is a big deal.

But that’s seen as taking money from an oil company. Yet wind and solar are huge items we forecast for also. So, does that put me in their pocket? Of course not. But it does to them. I found that out when I was making the Bill Nye movie as the villain. I was asked how much money I was getting from the Koch brothers because someone said they were paying me to say what I was saying. I have no idea who told them that, but I pointed to my 2007 Pontiac Firebird with a hole in the bumper and said, “How does a man getting rich off the Koch brothers drive that?” The fact is, if you did eliminate all non-wind and solar energy sources, that’s awesome for business. They need not only a seasonal forecast, but hour-by-hour forecasts. For instance, what does a 20-degree drop in a thunderstorm in Dallas do to demand? Or what if there is a prolonged heat wave in a big city, but the wind turbine source has light winds and is not producing? They need a forecast not only for an extended time period, but every day and every hour. Heck, why not just push wind and solar all the time if you are a forecaster? Now isn’t that an interesting question, as far as motivation goes? Mine is to look for trouble and forecast it, no matter who or what you are. I don’t care what your politics are. But think about this: Some people say you should care what someone’s politics are and question their profit motive. I suspect they are seeing in others what they know about themselves. In addition, there won’t be much of a profit motive anymore if the kind of draconian policies we see being touted come to pass (another leftist motivation).

articles.description: The latest draft political decision has left talks shaken, not stirred, with everyone in need of a stiff martini
paragraphs: Dr No In 2023 at COP28, nearly 200 countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. articles.title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
articles.description: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.
paragraphs: Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.
Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew , a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO .
It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.
Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.
There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.
Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions , the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.
This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.
This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño . However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

articles.title: Renewable Energy: Siting and Light Pollution Issues (eco-complaints)
articles.description: It is not easy being green. ‘Green’ energy has negative environmental consequences.
paragraphs: “Light pollution interrupts critical wildlife patterns for bats, migratory birds, insects (and more) and erodes biodiversity. In addition to these threats to wildlife, brighter night skies also threaten the health and natural cycles of humans, wastes energy and money, and disrupts ecosystems” according to a 2025 report from the World Economic Forum.” (- Haley Zaremba, below)

An article by Haley Zaremba (OilPrice.com) earlier this year, The Renewable Energy Transition Is Running Out of Places to Go (February 8, 2026), identified several issues of industrial wind complexes that seldom get attention. She speaks from the alarmist/transformationist camp, which makes her points extra interesting.

Just this month, a city-sized renewable energy development in Chile was scrapped after a year-long campaign led by astronomers who want to preserve the darkness of the Atacama Desert’s skies. The Atacama Desert is the highest and driest in the world, making it one of the world’s most ideal and important sites for astronomical observation. As of 2016, light pollution already covered nearly 80 percent of the planet , with a projected expansion of 2.2 percent a year . This means that a place like the Atacama is vanishingly rare. Chile’s highlands are therefore home to some of the biggest and most distinguished telescopes on the planet.

One of these, the European Southern Observatory’s (ESO’s) Paranal Observatory, would have been within five kilometers of the planned green energy site, which would occupy almost 7,500 acres (more than 3000 hectares). The ESO conducted a study on the likely impacts of this potential new neighbor and found that the megaproject would increase light pollution in the skies above the telescope by a minimum of 35 percent and increase atmospheric turbulence, further reducing clarity when observing the night sky. To nearly everyone’s surprise, the astronomers won … and the INNA (Integrated Energy Infrastructure Project for the Generation of Hydrogen and Green Ammonia) was scrapped.
“Light pollution,” Haley Zaremba concludes, “may sound like a relatively minor form of environmental degradation, but it can have serious consequences.” She explains:

Light pollution interrupts critical wildlife patterns for bats, migratory birds, insects (and more) and erodes biodiversity. In addition to these threats to wildlife, brighter night skies also threaten the health and natural cycles of humans, wastes energy and money, and disrupts ecosystems” according to a 2025 report from the World Economic Forum.

While this represents a major win for the astronomers and the sanctity of dark skies, renewable megaprojects have to go somewhere – and finding suitable sites for their construction is growing harder and harder. In developed countries, rural communities have been pushing back for years against massive-scale green energy projects in their areas, with relative success. And now, developing countries are starting to push back as well after years of bearing the brunt of these outsourced and offshored mega-developments, as well as their negative environmental and public health externalities.
