COP31 Electrification Absurdity: Australia Leads the Charge
articles.description: Australia is a terrible place to drive an EV, only beaten by places like Russia, Finland and Canada due to the impact of extreme cold on batteries.
paragraphs: Australia has given its 35×35 electrification pledge top billing in the opening days of COP31 in Türkiye. But will slow progress at home detract from its leadership role?

The launch overnight Tuesday of the Electrify Now Finance Coalition after what has been dubbed “ electrification day” at COP 31 in Antalya sees big plans to electrify cars, buildings and process heat, stretching the ambition of the summit to deliver concrete outcomes for industry.

The coalition’s launch coincides with COP31 president of negotiations and Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen’s efforts to secure a 35 per cent by 2035 global electrification pledge in the final decision text that negotiators will hammer out by the end of the two-week summit.

Despite scepticism that this year’s COP will deliver tangible outcomes, electrification experts like the Energy Efficiency Council head of electrification Anna Freeman , who is the global coordinator for the Electrify Global movement, are optimistic in both the potential to move the emissions needle by electrifying industry and to mobilise finance under the COP umbrella.

“It’s become clear that its a consumer-driven transition. It’s households and businesses including small business that are increasingly going to make the shift because they want predictability and affordability of their bills. That consumer understanding of the benefits of electrification are what’s going to carry business cases,” she said from the summit sidelines.

“Today, only around 22 per cent of Australia’s final energy demand is met by electricity. That means most of the energy we actually use in our homes, vehicles, businesses, farms, mines and factories still comes directly from fuels like petrol, diesel and gas, leaving us particularly exposed to volatile global energy markets.” …

Electrifying in a place like Australia is the height of absurdity. To be fair we get fewer blackouts than we used to, but I still keep two generators on standby, in case a storm takes down the power grid. And they can tear my gas cooker out of my cold dead hands, that gas cooker becomes pretty important when the power fails.
Here’s the full video of the screenshot above, just a short I filmed while going on a drive to clear my head. I’ve switched to 4WD and never intend to go back to normal vehicles.
I once tried driving a normal road vehicle on the rural road pictured in the video, I had to slow down to 15MPH – the road was tearing the vehicle apart.

articles.title: Our Health is Suffering Because of Global Warming, Say Lancet
articles.description: Unsurprisingly, the claim that heat killed 710,000 in 2023 is not based on actual data, but junk models.
paragraphs: For the tenth year running, it doubles down on the pretence that our health is suffering because of climate change and that people around the world are dropping like flies:

The past 11 years have been the hottest on record, and growing emissions mean overshooting the 1·5°C threshold is probably unavoidable—pushing the world beyond the limits needed to protect health. Indicators in this report show that, since the Paris Agreement entered into force in 2016, people have experienced not only increasing climate change-related health impacts and risks, but also an acceleration in these changes across numerous impacts compared with the previous decade. Although whether this acceleration will continue remains uncertain, it has already exacerbated adaptation challenges and claimed lives, harmed health, and affected wellbeing worldwide.

During 2016–23, heat was associated with an average of 540 800 deaths per year, of which 369 940 (68·4%) were attributable to human-caused climate change. Heat-related deaths reached a record-high of 710 000 estimated deaths globally in 2023, of which 71·5% can be attributed to climate change. Countries with a low human development index (HDI) had the highest proportion of heat-attributable deaths, reflecting the disproportionate adverse impacts of climate change on those least responsible for it, and the resulting amplification of global health inequities (indicator 1.1.5).

More frequent heatwaves and extreme droughts are increasingly threatening food security (indicator 1.4.1). Droughts affected 51·8% of global land for at least 1 month in 2025—the second-highest level recorded. This trend has accelerated, with the affected area growing 704% faster in 2016–25 than in 2006–15 (indicator 1.2.2). In parallel, the rate of increase in very extreme precipitation days, which in 2016–25 affected 17·2%% of global land annually, has also accelerated, exacerbating the risk and occurrence of health-threatening floods and landslides (indicator 1.2.3).

Rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns have also driven an accelerated increase in the environmental suitability for dengue virus transmission, and a record-high number of people (1·72 billion) lived within 100 km of coastal waters environmentally suitable for the transmission of Vibrio bacteria in 2025 (indicators 1.3.1 and 1.3.2). Climate change is also affecting malaria and West Nile virus transmission, reducing suitability in some areas while increasing it in others (indicator 1.3.1).
All of these silly claims have been debunked year after year, so this time I will focus on:

The Lancet Countdown claims there has been a large increase in drought conditions even in just the last ten years, itself a ludicrous statement, as the world’s climate does not change measurable on such short timescales.

articles.title: Under Trump, black lung disease is surging among Appalachia’s coal miners
articles.description: The administration’s attempt to revive the declining industry is leaving workers — and the planet — behind.
paragraphs: On President Donald Trump’s watch, a quiet epidemic has been left unchecked to prey upon Appalachia’s workforce. Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, the incurable progressive pulmonary disease better known as black lung, now affects 32% of longtime underground miners in Central Appalachia, which includes Kentucky, Virginia, and West Virginia.
That’s just one alarming statistic cited in a new report from Reimagine Appalachia, a coalition of organizations working to improve the lives of workers in Appalachia.

During Trump’s second term, his administration has taken an active role in weakening federal environmental regulations, handing over more land to mine operators, and privileging coal production over more renewable energy projects, while gutting a Biden-era rule meant to protect coal miners from black lung.

“The Trump administration has put substantive energy and funding toward expanding the coal industry without taking complementary actions to expand protections for the miners on whom the coal industry depends,” the report authors wrote.

A pet project of President Trump in his second term has been boosting what he calls “beautiful, clean coal.” The administration has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into new coal facilities, and Trump has bragged that “the United States is opening up new mines at the fastest pace since the 1950s.”

Demand for coal has continued to decline, but its extraction helps fuel climate change. As recently as 2024 , coal was responsible for almost half of all carbon dioxide emissions from U.S. electricity generation, while providing only 15% of its power. Both underground and surface coal mining operations release climate-warming methane into the atmosphere.
Meanwhile, black lung cases have increased more than 60% since 2018, to the highest rates since 1978.

For decades, coal dust presented the greatest danger to miners’ respiratory health; mine operators did little to prevent its spread, and generations of workers fell victim to the demon of the coalfields. After the passage of the 1969 Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act , which introduced a federal coal dust exposure limit as well as robust safety standards and engineering controls, the rate of black lung cases dropped by 90%.

In 1974, the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommended a stricter limit for the respirable crystalline silica that causes black lung disease. The Institute stated that miners should not be exposed to more than 50 micrograms per cubic meter during any 10-hour shift of a 40-hour work week, noting that compliance ​“should prevent adverse effects of crystalline silica.”

But the current limit, which was implemented in the 1970s, is still twice that – and that’s assuming mine operators comply. The permissible silica exposure threshold for coal miners remains double that of every other industry, including construction.

articles.title: Countries take up industry push to loosen UN carbon market rules at COP31
articles.description: A draft decision reflects demands from dozens of countries to reassess the UN carbon market’s integrity rules, a push campaigners blame on industry lobbying.
paragraphs: Dozens of countries - from big emerging economies to the world's poorest nations - are calling for the UN's new carbon market to reassess climate integrity rules, in a push that campaigners and researchers have blamed on industry lobbying.

At COP31 talks on the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) this weekend, the Like-Minded Developing Countries – a group that includes Saudi Arabia, India and China – the Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and landlocked developing countries raised concerns about the requirements project developers must meet, according to sources familiar with the closed-door discussions.

They warned about the cumulative weight of those requirements developed under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as barriers to implementation. Several countries, including Singapore and some Latin American states, said rules must keep projects financially viable, while South Korea asked for proportionate requirements, the sources said.

They warned about the cumulative weight of those requirements developed under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as barriers to implementation. Several countries, including Singapore and some Latin American states, said rules must keep projects financially viable, while South Korea asked for proportionate requirements, the sources said.

Their demands closely track arguments from carbon market industry groups, which claim PACM's conservative approach to counting emission reductions is so strict that few projects will ever come to fruition.

In a letter published ahead of COP31, the lobby groups asked governments to "raise implementation concerns" and to request that the Supervisory Body - the UN body that oversees the market - assess the "combined impact" of its rules on the feasibility of projects.

The letter was signed by the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), a business group whose members include fossil fuel giants Shell, BP, Saudi Aramco and Chevron, along with the Project Developer Forum and the Wildlife Conservation Society, which develops forest conservation programmes.

Those demands are reflected in the first draft of the COP31 decision on the mechanism, published late on Saturday. To guard against over-crediting, PACM’s rules deliberately err on the side of issuing fewer credits when emissions cuts from projects are uncertain.

articles.title: Why the Electrification Push at Global Climate Talks Is Stalling
COP31’s electricity goal must be about more than AI and luxuries for the rich
articles.description: The pledge to boost electrification must not neglect the pressing need to bring clean, affordable power to hundreds of millions of people still living without it
paragraphs: International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol celebrates the electricity demands of AI and electric cars, but the revolution must be about more than luxuries for the rich. It must bring clean, affordable power to the hundreds of millions still living without it.

The world is entering the age of electrification. But while wealthy countries focus on powering AI data centres, electric cars and other energy-hungry technologies, hundreds of millions of people across Africa and the developing world still lack access to electricity.

International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol celebrates the electricity demands of AI and electric cars, but the revolution must be about more than luxuries for the rich. It must bring clean, affordable power to the hundreds of millions still living without it.

The world is entering the age of electrification. But while wealthy countries focus on powering AI data centres, electric cars and other energy-hungry technologies, hundreds of millions of people across Africa and the developing world still lack access to electricity.
The real promise of the electricity revolution is not simply meeting the growing demands of those who already have plenty, but bringing clean, affordable power to those who have none.

So the decision by Türkiye and Australia to make electrification a flagship initiative at COP31 should be welcomed. Their proposed 35 by 35 goal , increasing electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, could accelerate this transformation.

But who is this revolution actually for? Birol has celebrated the arrival of the electricity age, identifying AI data centres, electric transport and air conditioning as three major drivers of growing electricity demand.

Cincinnati prepares for climate migrants
articles.description: The Ohio municipality became the first U.S. city to release a climate migration readiness plan.
paragraphs: As seas rise and wildfires and hurricanes grow more intense, some people are asking where they could move to reduce their vulnerability.
Cincinnati is one of several northern inland cities promoting itself as a potential destination. This year, it became the first U.S. city to release a climate migration readiness plan .
Tim Robustelli is with the Future of Land and Housing program at New America, a think tank. He says an influx of new residents could bring many benefits.
Robustelli: “Economic development, entrepreneurship, and of course, with more economic activity with larger populations, that’s a larger tax base.”
But he says as Cincinnati and other cities plan to attract and support new residents, they also need to protect current residents from being left behind or pushed out.
For example, cities can provide rental assistance and create policies that protect tenants from eviction if property values rise.
Robustelli: “Other tools like property tax breaks … can sort of help offset some of the increased costs you see with redevelopment and gentrification.”
And he says grants and low-interest loans can help people pay for critical home repairs so they can stay in their homes long-term.
So cities can welcome new residents and support those who have lived there for generations.

articles.title: COP31 Bulletin Day 7: Incoming ministers set to battle over cover text
articles.description: A first draft of the Antalya summit's main political outcome includes a wide range of asks from 160 countries and must be whittled down amid divisions over science, finance and energy transition
paragraphs: The second week of the UN climate conference in Antalya has opened with a sober outlook, as fossil-fuel producers and large developing countries push back strongly against some of the key anticipated outcomes from the talks. Ministers will need to work hard to resolve differences, COP watchers said.

In a late-night stocktaking session on Saturday, the groups of Arab and Like-Minded Developing Countries - which includes powerful emerging economies - said they did not want to see new sectoral targets included in the cover decision. That’s a reference to the electrification pledge proposed by the Turkish presidency, now reportedly backed by 30 nations though a list has yet to be made available.

In addition, Saudi Arabia rejected moves to reference Brazil’s global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, while India opposed mentioning scientific reports and findings “external” to the UN process. Those include a recent report from the UN Environment Programme on how to deal with an inevitable overshoot of the 1.5C warming limit.

That’s a reference to the electrification pledge proposed by the Turkish presidency, now reportedly backed by 30 nations though a list has yet to be made available.

In addition, Saudi Arabia rejected moves to reference Brazil’s global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, while India opposed mentioning scientific reports and findings “external” to the UN process. Those include a recent report from the UN Environment Programme on how to deal with an inevitable overshoot of the 1.5C warming limit.

These groups of countries, along with Russia, Argentina and African nations, also objected to ongoing consultations over reforms to the UN climate process to make it more effective, saying there was no consensus on proposals so far and they should be kept out of the cover decision too.

Experts said the sharp divisions would be hard to reconcile in time to land an ambitious cover decision. Alden Meyer, senior associate at E3G, told journalists the co-presidency of Türkiye and Australia is “under growing pressure to both clarify how the formal negotiations, the cover decision and the Action Agenda initiatives on electrification, in particular, fit together, and to resolve the deep splits on many issues”.

articles.title: A Battle Over Science Risks Jeopardizing Climate Talks for Years
Climate Diplomacy Brief: COP31 day 7
articles.description: Australia, Türkiye have 5 days to avoid the diplomatic equivalent of falling into an ornamental pond fully clothed
paragraphs: Damp squib If there’s an image that sums up COP31 so far it’s this man falling into an ornamental pool at the venue (poor guy). Traps lie everywhere for the somewhat hapless Australian & Turkish co-hosts in week 2 of this summit. An electrification deal pushed by Ankara had 30 signatures on Saturday. The cover text marshalled by Australia was a Christmas list last week. A new iteration is mooted to land on Monday/Tuesday. Divan In South Africa it was an Indaba. In Brazil a Mutirao. In Glasgow a pint of Tennents and a fish supper. The name given to the ministerial gathering at COP31 is a ‘Divan’, which is an Ottoman term for Imperial Assembly. Early on Saturday, COP boss Kurum said talks would be split into 4 streams : ministerial engagement, presidency consultations, ministerial consultations on outstanding political issues, and technical negotiations.

Ministers Arriving ministers get to work on Monday and address the ‘high level’ segment tomorrow. Over 112 ministers are listed, with the main negotiating groups taking the floor on 16 Nov. This is where we’ll get a good sense of (i) how many have signed up to the Turkish electrification target (ii) how many want to stipulate it should be clean (iii) who wants a strong cover text (iv) who wants the IPCC to deliver its blockbuster AR7 report in 2028. Bookmarks *IEA: Energy crisis policy tracker *Carbon Brief: Who wants what at COP31? *Carbon Brief: Negotiating text tracker *NRDC: International climate finance tracker *CAT: GHG analysis of all major emitters *ENB: Priceless daily update from inside the talks Vibes: Saturday’s plenary Here’s a taster of how week 1 wrapped in the closing mid-week plenary:

*Arab Group: Wants no top-down targets or naming of sectors/energy sources *Argentina: Complained about the approach to week 2 *EU: Pushed hard on 1.5C overshoot and the need for a better mitigation plan *Iraq: Don’t target sectors / add new requirements (the whole point of talks?) *LMDCs: Worried about inclusivity in week 2 with so many side hustle groups *Russia: Blocking oceans in cover text, complained about the approach to week 2 *Switzerland: Stressed about 1.5C overshoot *Umbrella Group: Disappointed with mitigation progress, want better this week

Kurum: Lowballing COP boss Kurum’s presser on Saturday dampened expectations. Just 30 countries have signed the electrification pledge, he said, although more would follow. He spoke of “enormous support” for work at COP31 without offering much evidence. Quizzed by two journalists on how fossil fuels would be addressed, he said it had been stipulated in a previous decision and told the media not to concentrate on empty promises or insignificant words. Bowen: Spitballing In contrast, COP negotiations boss Bowen - fresh from offering the world tips on where to store mobile phones - exuded confidence. He talked of work across 160 “items” in 60 “mandates” and spoke of a new cover text landing on Monday/Tuesday that would send a “message” to boardrooms. The ministerial pairs (below) will be key to delivering an outcome, he added.

articles.title: Climate Diplomacy Brief
articles.description: ‘Choose the future and never give up,’ Guterres tells delegates as COP shuffles on
paragraphs: MIA Is there anyone in the cockpit? A week into COP31 and there’s a definite sense of drift. The co-hosts are lying low, work on a main political/cover text seems a mess (even containing reference to the “ largely defunct ” Kyoto Protocol) and levels of support for the 35% by 2035 electrification deal are a mystery. Silence is not unusual but it’s a little worrying. Maybe they’ve been learning a new dance ( like this ). Choreography next week is key. Wrap Saturday usually sees a marked shift in gear at COPs as ministers arrive and the main negotiating venues of week 1 (SBI & SBSTA) formally close. UN climate boss Simon ‘no silver bullet’ Stiell’s 10:30 presser and the 13:00 Presidency briefing will offer a vibe check. It’s unclear if we’ll see fireworks or everyone exude hammam chill in plenary sessions as envoys debate adaptation finance, 1.5C overshoot, GST2 and the IPCC. Bonus We made it through Friday 13th without the world reaching infinity population, as predicted by the journal Science back in 1960. Turns out Australia PM Albanese and his environment minister/COP co-boss Bowen have a theory why that’s the case. The pair were caught live on air discussing the danger of phone radiation on their penises . “My d**k, that’s rather important, arguably more important than the heart,” said Bowen.

Socks Beware COPs bearing gifts. In 2015 at the Paris Agreement the media got a tote bag. In 2021 in Glasgow it was a can of Irn-Bru and a deep fried pizza. In 2026 the bribes - sorry gifts - are next level. Bags, bottles, laptop stands, magnets, lapel pins, cuddly toys and two pairs of socks, which hopefully isn’t a sign we’re going to run over next weekend. We asked our Turkish colleague and he promised the power bank probably won't be bugged. Bookmarks *IEA: Energy crisis policy tracker *Carbon Brief: Who wants what at COP31? *Carbon Brief: Negotiating text tracker *NRDC: International climate finance tracker *CAT: GHG analysis of all major emitters *ENB: Priceless daily update from inside the talks Sitrep So where are we as week 1 wraps? Here’s our traffic-light take. COP veterans won’t be shocked that we’re mostly on red, amber at best. 1. Is finance allocated by COP31 to Nepal for reconstruction/early warning ? 2. Is there a clean electrification goal ? Does it include $$$, grids & policies? 3. Are new fossil fuel phaseout plans published by governments? 4. Will hosts Türkiye & Australia commit to curbing coal use/exports ? 5. Is there an agreed plan to triple adaptation finance (as agreed in 2025)? 6. Have countries agreed (in negotiations) on how Global Stocktake 2 will work? 7. Will the IPCC deliver its next blockbuster report by GST2/2028?

We mulled over what song would be totally out of keeping with the last week, and Lindsay chose her favourite tune of all time: ‘Tubthumping’ by Chumbawunba . Comments as ever to Lindsay.smith@gsccnetwork.org .

articles.title: Ironworkers in high demand as wind energy booms
articles.description: Illinois’ Climate Works Pre-Apprenticeship Program provides people from underserved communities with free training.
paragraphs: In an iconic photo from the 1930s, ironworkers eat lunch, perched on the steel beam of a skyscraper. The photo documents the critical role these tradesmen played in building city skylines.
And now, ironworkers are also essential for building another kind of tall tower – wind turbines.
Noah Mihaly, a union ironworker for White Construction, is helping build the Coles Wind Farm in Illinois.
Mihaly: “It’s almost entirely ironworkers that are preparing the engine rooms, preparing the blades … and then putting together all the pieces, as well as constructing the foundations.”
Given their vital role in building wind farms, ironworkers are in high demand as the clean energy industry expands.
So to recruit and prepare more people for these jobs, Illinois established a workforce training program under the state’s Climate and Equitable Jobs Act.
Called the Climate Works Pre-Apprenticeship Program, it provides people from underserved areas with free training and help applying to apprenticeships.
Mihaly: “The pre-apprenticeship program was my jumpstart. It was the main reason I was able to get into the ironworker’s union.”

articles.title: Climate Diplomacy Brief
articles.description: Cover text Christmas list lands, cash debate heats up, electrification numbers mount
paragraphs: Catnip It says much about events at COP31 on Thursday that a Turkish news agency decided to attach a camera to a cat and allow it to prowl through the venue. AI or not it was one of the more interesting events of a day that promised much and delivered little. At least the trams into the venue seem to work, while the volunteers doling out bananas and chocolate are a rare winning move from the hosts. Hopefully the cat didn’t fall asleep in a side event. Covers A ‘ summary of reflections ’ on what might make a final cover/political/Antalya Declaration landed overnight. Much like the Christmas wishlist my kids handed me mid-October, it’s a list of everything everyone wants and thus won’t get. Would a ‘text’ with these elements be any stronger than the 2023 ‘Global Stocktake’ that set the bar for fossil fuel phaseout? Will it send a market signal? Questions envoys will need to mull.

Sitrep The two-day leaders’ meeting has held up the ‘negotiations’ so it’s no shock there’s been limited progress. The arrival of ministers over the weekend will help. Adaptation cash is central to any deal. Behind the scenes, numbers on an electrification deal seem to be rising: IEA boss Birol’s presser at 16:30 may have more on that. Some observers say China has been quietly constructive. One to watch, even if they’re now not keen on hosting COP33 in 2028. Ministerial pairs Adaptation: Sierra Leone & UK Finance: France & Philippines Mitigation: Germany & India Just Transition: Mexico & Poland Ocean: Canada & Palau

Deaf Did anyone pay attention to Lula’s Wednesday speech? Türkiye and Australia were keen to laud an 83-year-old who’s just bagged a 4th term in office. As to his plea for the co-hosts to take ownership of the three COP31 roadmaps on finance, fossil fuels and forests: zilch. The Aussies, so keen to assert their Pacific roots, seem far less keen to actually do anything substantive to help small islands, as this video outlines . Goal Lula also offered to host a conference to phase down fossil fuels, telling civil society reps: “We have a moral obligation.” The offer came in response to a request from Brazil’s Climate Observatory. Tuvalu and Ireland will co-host the next edition in 2027. First Brazil needs to land its own plan to phase down fossil fuel use, which will entail conversations with giant state oil company Petrobras. Howler Andy Burnham is no Harry Kane. On the day the Ballon D’or winner became England’s most capped player , his country’s PM was through on a COP goal… and blasted it over the bar, ala Everton’s Dele Alli in 2022. The UK was well placed to deliver a fossil fuel phaseout plan at COP31. Instead, No.10 compiled a series of electrification measures, branded it a ‘roadmap’ and tried to sell it as such.

GST: What/why/when The Global Stocktake takes place every 5 years. The first was at COP28 (2023), the second will be at COP33 (2028). It’s the main lever of the Paris Agreement, where progress on global action is presented and a plan to tackle gaps is agreed. Work on GST2 has started with a ‘high level’ event on 18 Nov, but countries have to agree here how it will work. For example, how is 1.5C overshoot addressed and how will fossil roadmaps be dealt with?

articles.title: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions
articles.description: UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband in Antalya spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.
paragraphs: UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.

Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels .
Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”.
Pushing back on a question about COP reform, Miliband explained how he is “quite pro the institution of the COP”, given its role in bringing countries together for climate action.
He emphasised the importance of action on methane and the UK’s “support” for the “35×35” electrification pledge .
Carbon Brief: Well, thanks very much for joining us. I know you’re very busy and we’ve got some reader questions. It’s great that you’ve got time to answer some.
CB: How, in your experience at COP31 so far, has the UK’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field and the rumoured rollback of its EV targets affected the UK’s standing as a climate leader?

EM: People see us as showing leadership. People don’t see us as rolling back, and I think what people see is a government that is driving the agenda on electrification and clean power. Because after all, we have a clean power 2030 target, which is world-leading.
[We] have the most ambitious targets on net-zero, the [ nationally determined contributions ] NDCs, of frankly, any country in the world. [We] are legislating for no new oil and gas licences.

And what I’m trying to do here is also bring a new dimension to this, which is the whole national security dimension. Because I think, if you’re serious about national security, you need to be serious about climate. And those parties – and those people – who aren’t serious about climate, I don’t think they’re serious about national security. Because this is a national security issue for, I think – frankly – every government across the world.

articles.title: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
articles.description: The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
paragraphs: Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “ climate finance ” and have traditionally announced multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.
Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.
A civil-society tracker shows that only six nations have announced new multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.
Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out plans for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.
Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new funds.
As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for new finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.
Under the Paris Agreement , developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.
This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks , UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.

paragraphs: Access “If you’re not here already, you won’t get in until this afternoon.” Security were closing gates into the COP venue just after 7am this morning, reports Carbon Brief’s Simon Evans. Few will be playing tiny violins for delegates. Bad things are happening everywhere. But telling the media & civil society to travel between 5-7am to allow 100+ world leaders a nice trip is unusual. A sign of who organisers believe matters. It limits access & coverage. The host country agreement demands better. Bosstown The 11-12 Nov leaders segment is central to the Türkiye/Australia plan to leave COP31 with an electrification deal. Speakers on Wednesday - doubtless refreshed after a quick ride along empty roads into HQ - include Brazil’s Lula, China VP Zheng Han, the EU’s VDL, Saudi’s MBS, Mia Mottely from Barbados and heads of state from Marshall Islands, Sierra Leone and Liberia. Türkiye President Erdogan - fresh from opening two new oil fields - is also in town.

** 14:30 - leaders’ speeches start** Strategy Türkiye’s priorities for COP are clear from the 11-12 Nov plan . The [insert ‘clean’ into cover text] electrification goal of 35% of final energy use to be electricity by 2035, the growth of green industry (co-chaired by Egypt, Germany and the UK) and a zero waste session chaired by Türkiye’s first lady. Odd fact: Türkiye imported 510,000 tonnes of plastic waste from the EU last year, only 10% of which was recycled.

Roadmaps: Who said what *Brazil: Planning is a good thing. So let’s start planning. *Africa Group: We’re just 4% of global emissions. We need support to transition fairly. *UK: Don’t need new negotiations or new bodies or new mechanisms. *South Africa: Cheap renewables make the transition from fossil fuels possible. *Nigeria: This is all about investment opportunities. *Germany: Need to accelerate electrifying mobility, heating and industrial processes. *Netherlands: Committing an additional €6m to a transition fund for roadmap planning COP cover Australia’s Bowen will consult Parties on a political cover decision until Friday, then publish a summary and ask for written inputs by Saturday night, with the aim of releasing a first draft early in week two. Consultations will focus on (i) what recent progress and developments could the cover decision recognise, (ii) impacts, challenges and opportunities we face in the world, (iii) how can we work together to accelerate implementation. COP boss “If there was any doubt, it is clear that Murat and only Murat holds the gavel.” This post on power dynamics at COP31 by veteran observer Joanna Depledge based on Tuesday’s handover ceremony is worth a read. “Murat’s first act as President was to invite Bowen to the podium, underlining Bowen’s key role, but also confirming Murat at the top of the authority hierarchy,” Depledge writes.

articles.title: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?
articles.description: More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, potentially making it the largest COP in history.
paragraphs: Carbon Brief analysis of the provisional lists of delegates, published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), reveals that more than 14,000 delegates have been registered as “host country guests”.
For comparison, the final list for COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year included only around 1,300 delegates in this category.
As with COP30 , Donald Trump’s US government has not sent a delegation. Other no-shows include Israel and Myanmar.

It was reported ahead of the summit that Taliban officials from Afghanistan had been registered for the event as observers; however, there are no delegates from observer states in the provisional lists.
With more than 3,000 “virtual” delegates signed up to attend the summit online, the total number of people registered for the event surpasses 95,000.
With 92,934 participants registered, COP31 is provisionally the largest COP in history – topping COP28 in Dubai , which was attended by more than 80,000 people.

This total is based on the delegates that have registered to be at the summit in person. The UNFCCC releases the final figures – based on participants collecting a physical badge at the venue – after the summit has ended.
The chart below shows how the provisional figures for COP31 compare to the final totals in previous COPs – going back to COP1 in Berlin in 1995.

The participant lists provided by the UNFCCC are divided between the different types of groups and organisations attending the summit. The largest group at COP31 is for delegates representing parties. These are nation-states, plus the European Union, that have ratified the convention and play a full part in negotiations.

articles.title: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use
articles.description: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn…
paragraphs: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project .

The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today , says that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.
This is primarily driven by peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia and is linked to the development of a strong El Niño event this year.
As a result, total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and land use are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026 – marginally above 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

Research published alongside the report by the same team in Nature Climate Change finds that the growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles (EVs) now offsets around two-thirds of the emissions that would otherwise come from rising energy demand.
However, the deployment of these technologies is not yet enough to push global emissions into a sustained decline, according to the study.
(For more on previous editions of the Global Carbon Project’s annual report, see Carbon Brief’s coverage in 2025 , 2024 , 2023 and 2022 .)
Total global CO2 emissions, which combines fossil fuels and land-use change, are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.
The increase in 2026 comes entirely from a projected rise in land-use emissions, which are more challenging to estimate than fossil emissions.

articles.title: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
articles.description: Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31
paragraphs: One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a “just transition mechanism”.
This follows years of calls from civil society to support a “ just transition ” as countries shift towards low-emissions energy systems and away from fossil fuels.
At the COP30 UN climate talks last year in the Brazilian city of Belém parties agreed to establish a “mechanism” to support this goal, called the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” (BAM).
Groups that have championed the BAM want it to act as a central hub on just transitions, providing support for workers and communities around the world.
However, the details of exactly what the much-touted BAM will consist of remain vague, with developed and developing countries disagreeing about its functions and purpose.
Disagreements continued at the UN climate talks in Bonn in June 2026, including on the crucial question of how the BAM will be financed.
Here, Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31.
A “ just transition ” is the idea that workers and communities should be supported in the shift to a low-carbon economy. It is a central principle behind the idea of climate justice .
Often, the term refers to those linked to the fossil-fuel industry, but it can also refer to transitions taking place in agriculture , heavy industry and various other sectors.
The concept originated in the 1980s, when US labour unions forged alliances with environmental justice groups. It has since become a key part of international climate discussions.

articles.title: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
articles.description: The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
paragraphs: That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “ state of the climate ” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets. Dr Zeke Hausfather , Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ ask me anything ” session.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.

This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.
The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.

Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”
On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.
Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.
Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.

articles.title: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
articles.description: China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
paragraphs: This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.
The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.
The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “ flat or falling ” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.
The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown .
Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “ wasted ” wind and solar fell.

Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.

The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates . This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.

Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.

articles.title: ECMWF and the Copernicus Climate and Atmosphere services at COP31 in Antalya
articles.description: ECMWF and the Copernicus Climate and Atmosphere services at COP31 in Antalya Sonia 2nd November 2026 The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the Copernicus services it operates on behalf of the European Commission will be present at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. The world comes together on 9 – 20 November 2026 to discuss climate change, and the present and future mitigation and adaptation strategies. ECMWF holds the official status of observer of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) as an Intergovernmental Organization since 2023. The wider
paragraphs: The wider ECMWF, the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) and the Copernicus Climate Change Service (CAMS) will be well represented in Antalya. ECMWF Director-General Florian Pappenberger, Irina Sandu, Deputy Director-General and Director of Science and Innovation at ECMWF, the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Director Carlo Buontempo and Laurence Rouil, Director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) as well as Vincent-Henri Peuch, Director for ECMWF Engagement with the EU will participate in the conference.

The top-level ECMWF delegation will highlight the value of open, high quality and operational weather, climate and atmosphere data, and actionable information in helping protect lives and livelihoods, as climate change looms. The latest advances in artificial intelligence-based models, the value of ongoing cooperation with ECMWF Member and Cooperating states and the new projects and applications released by the Centre and its partners are some of the key topics that will be discussed in Antalya.
On 6 November, C3S will release its Climate Bulletin for October with a preliminary assessment of the annual global temperatures for 2026.

From the start of COP31, on 9 November, ECMWF Director-General Florian Pappenberger will participate in a joint event with the Turkish State Meteorological Service and the World Meteorological Organization on the Systematic Observations Financing Facility (SOFF).

Türkiye is a full Member State of ECMWF and has been since its early beginnings. The meeting will also be attended by WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. ECMWF is an active player of the United Nations SOFF initiative by providing data and dedicated research efforts, in addition to helping promote the initiative.
On the same day, Vincent-Henri Peuch will represent ECMWF at the Earth Information Day organised by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.

Deputy Director-General of ECMWF Irina Sandu will discuss the value of impact-based forecasts at a session organised by hosts Turkish Meteorological Service and the Azerbaijan National Hydrometeorological Service on 11 November.

On 10 November ECMWF is organising a session in the joint Multilateral Development Banks Pavilion presenting the upcoming ClimateSET application , developed by the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) in cooperation with the European Investment Bank (EIB). As global warming increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, climate information is becoming also essential for investment decisions; the new tool supports initial climate risk assessment for the financial sector.

articles.title: September 2026 Temperature Update
articles.description: August 2026 was the warmest August on record. El Niño is strengthening rapidly and expected to break all-time records. 2026 is likely to be a new record warmest year.
paragraphs: The following is a summary of global temperature conditions in Berkeley Earth’s analysis of September 2026.

According to Berkeley Earth’s high-resolution temperature dataset, September 2026 was the 2 nd warmest September since records began in 1850, with a monthly global average of 1.65 ± 0.11 °C (2.96 ± 0.19 °F) above the 1850–1900 (pre-industrial) average. It sits about 0.06 °C below September 2023. The anomaly in September 2026 is nominally the third largest of any month, behind only September 2023 and August 2026.

On a month-to-month basis, September was nominally slightly cooler than August 2026 though within the margin or error. It remains sharply warmer than other months in 2026. September 2026 continued the run of months above the 1.5 °C mark that began in July, as the warming influence of El Niño has grown.

Only one month of 2026 has set a record warm month (August 2026) with most months entering as the 2 nd to 5 th warmest. Depsite that, we have now pushed close to all-time record high temperature anomalies. Record and near-record warmth is expected to continue through the end of the year due to the short-term influence of a record-breaking El Niño.

Over the most recent 12 months (October 2025 to September 2026), the global average was 1.458 ± 0.074 °C (2.62 ± 0.13 °F) above the 1850–1900 average, making it the 2 nd warmest such 12-month period on record. It is behind the period ending in September 2024 and effectively tied with the period ending in September 2025, which it exceeds by only 0.003 °C. Because El Niño’s influence on the global mean lags its peak in the Pacific, this measure is expected to keep rising into 2027.

In September 2026, warmer-than-average temperatures covered most of the globe. The warmth was most pronounced across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, where El Niño appears as a broad warm band stretching east to the coast of South America, and across the high Arctic, including the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. Large positive anomalies also covered western and central Europe and the western Mediterranean, the western North Atlantic off North America, Australia, and much of northern and central Asia. Some of the largest anomalies anywhere were over West Antarctica. The most prominent cool anomaly was elsewhere on Antarctica, centered on the Weddell Sea sector and stretching along parts of the East Antarctic coast, with smaller cool areas over the Greenland ice sheet, along the west coast of the United States, and at the southern tip of South America.

Roughly 11.5% of Earth’s surface experienced its locally warmest September on record (about 9.3% of land and 12.7% of ocean surfaces), and 80.3% of the surface was warmer than average. The largest contiguous region of record warmth occurred in the Eastern tropical Pacific, where a record-breaking El Niño event is underway. Record warmth also covered parts of the tropical and western North Atlantic including the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean, Iberia and the western Mediterranean, northwest Africa, the Sahel and the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and the Persian Gulf, much of the Indian Ocean, maritime Southeast Asia, and parts of northern Russia and Kazakhstan. Record and near-record warmth in tropical South America, Africa, and Southeast Asia are common features during large El Niño events.

articles.title: Introducing Berkeley Earth’s Data Pipeline 2.0
articles.description: A rebuilt, expanded and more resilient foundation for the Berkeley Earth temperature record. For fifteen years stakeholders from across the climate, resilience, and research ecosystems have come to Berkeley Earth for a clear, transparent, and trustworthy read on how our climate is changing. Much of that trust rests on work that has, until very recently,…
paragraphs: For fifteen years stakeholders from across the climate, resilience, and research ecosystems have come to Berkeley Earth for a clear, transparent, and trustworthy read on how our climate is changing. Much of that trust rests on work that has, until very recently, remained relatively invisible: the data pipeline that gathers, merges, and quality-checks millions of observations from more than 50,000 global weather stations every month.

Following a number of upstream data disruptions last year, Berkeley Earth made a commitment to invest in building a more resilient and robust data pipeline, one less dependent on any one single upstream source of observations, and one that could maintain crucial data continuity in the case that any single ingest product was disrupted or lost.

Today we’re excited to announce the launch of Berkeley Earth’s newly rebuilt pipeline 2.0 , not only reinforced but expanded to provide not only the most comprehensive but also the most resilient observational temperature record available. Below is an overview of what we improved, what hasn’t changed, and why this matters for the greater climate and resilience ecosystem.

The rebuilt pipeline is faster by design, which means earlier monthly updates going forward, and we expect to have near-real-time data flowing into Synthesis , our high-resolution climate platform, available within the next few months.
